sections.html:
Gardner is a Johnson County city in the southwest corner of the Kansas City metro. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 26,154 residents, up 12.0 percent from 23,349 in April 2020. The city covers about 10 square miles, with Gardner Lake on the north side and the headwaters of Kill Creek, which runs north to meet the Kansas River at De Soto.

Gardner works as a commuter town. The mean trip to work is 22.9 minutes, so buyers tend to ask first about routes into the rest of the metro.

sections.h2: How Gardner grew from a trail junction to a suburb
sections.html:
Free-State settlers founded Gardner in 1857, at the point where the Santa Fe Trail split from the Oregon and California Trails. It was named for Henry Gardner, then governor of Massachusetts, and got its first post office in 1858. The town had only 676 people in 1950.

Growth came late and fast. The count was 3,191 in 1990, 9,396 in 2000, 19,123 in 2010 and 23,287 in 2020. Much of the housing therefore went up inside a short span, and plenty of houses share an age and a set of systems. An owner whose roof, water heater and furnace were all installed around the same time may face several replacements in the same few years, which can weigh on a sale.

A given house can land far above or below the median, depending on its age, lot, condition and school zone.

USD 231 is the largest local employer, with 926 people. Walmart, Cosentino's Price Chopper, Meadowbrook Rehabilitation Hospital, Excelligence Learning Corp and the City of Gardner each employ between 165 and 225. Plenty of residents work elsewhere in the metro, and a BNSF Railway fueling plant and office in nearby Edgerton, about 3 miles from western Gardner, employs about 200.

USD 231 runs six of its seven elementary schools inside Gardner, along with Wheatridge, Trail Ridge and Pioneer Ridge middle schools and Gardner Edgerton High School. Many families begin their search with school boundaries, so learn which elementary school your address feeds.

sections.h2: How does Gardner's weather affect a house?
sections.html:
Summers are hot and humid and winters are mild to cool. Rainfall averages 37.54 inches a year at the New Century AirCenter station, with May and June the wettest months. Records there include 114 degrees in July and minus 15 in February.

Spring rain, summer heat and hard freezes all test gutters, grading, sump pumps and roofing.

  • Point downspouts away from the foundation, since spring rain is the heaviest of the year.
  • Check attic ventilation and insulation, because hot summers and cold snaps load the cooling and heating system.
  • A basement with water stains will be found by a buyer's inspector. Decide ahead of time how you will disclose and price it.

The city supplies its own electric, water and wastewater service, which means a sale touches city hall and not only the county. The account holder must appear in person at City Hall, 120 East Main Street, to transfer service. The connection fee is $10 per service or $15 for both. To stop service, contact the office before 3 p.m. on the day service should end.

sections.h2: Permits for work you have done
sections.html:
Gardner requires building permits for projects such as finishing a basement, re-roofing, setting a shed, installing a sprinkler system or pool, and building a fence or deck. Contractors must hold a Johnson County Contractor's license, except fence and irrigation contractors, and homeowners who did the work themselves file a Statement of Homeowner Installation.

A buyer's inspector or lender may ask about permits for a finished basement or a new roof. Pull together whatever paperwork you hold ahead of listing day. Missing a permit for older work is fixable: tell the buyer, then ask the city's Building and Inspections office what is on file.

sections.h2: Deeds and property tax in Johnson County
sections.html:
Gardner deeds are recorded at the Johnson County Register of Deeds in Olathe, at 111 S. Cherry St. The fee is $21 for the first page of a deed or mortgage and $17 for each added page. Filing the sales validation questionnaire that Kansas requires with most deeds costs nothing under K.S.A. 79-1437c.

  • Johnson County takes eRecording at no extra fee.
  • Pay the whole bill or the first half by December 20. The second half follows on May 10.
  • Notices of value go out by March 1. If you disagree, the informal meeting with the county appraiser must happen by May 15.

At closing the title company handles the tax split between you and the buyer. When you sell in spring, expect a line showing whether the second half is settled and how the rest is divided.

sections.h2: What do Gardner sellers usually face?
sections.html:
Most owners are choosing between a listing with showings and repairs and a quicker sale as is. The usual reasons:

  • A short timeline. A job change inside the metro or farther away leaves little time for staging and open houses.
  • Deferred maintenance. Houses built in the same years can reach roof and mechanical replacement age together.
  • Inherited houses. Heirs in other states may want one closing instead of months of upkeep.
  • Rentals. About one in three Gardner homes is renter-occupied, and owners who rent a house out sometimes decide to sell.

A cash offer fits those cases if you accept that a buyer pricing in repairs may offer less than a fully renovated listing would bring. Compare the offer with a listing's costs and wait time, then decide.

An agent's client, a family or a company, the same questions protect you.

  • Is the offer for cash, and can the buyer show proof of funds?
  • Who orders and pays for the title search and closing, and which title company handles it?
  • Is the house bought as is, and are inspections limited to a short window?
  • What closing date is offered, and can it move if you need more time to move out?
  • Will you be asked to sign anything before you see a written offer?

Written answers let you compare a cash offer, a listing and a sale by owner on the same terms. Asking costs you nothing.

faqs.q: How many people live in Gardner, KS?
faqs.a: An estimated 26,154 residents as of July 1, 2025. That is up from 23,287 at the 2020 census and 19,123 in 2010.

faqs.q: Which county is Gardner in, and where do I record a deed?
faqs.a: Gardner is in Johnson County. Deeds are recorded with the Johnson County Register of Deeds, 111 S. Cherry St., Olathe. Most deeds need a real estate sales validation questionnaire under K.S.A. 79-1437c.

faqs.q: How do I transfer my Gardner utilities when I sell?
faqs.a: Gardner provides water, wastewater and electric service itself. To transfer, the account holder visits City Hall in person and pays $10 per service or $15 for both. To end service, contact City Hall before 3 p.m. on the day.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for work I did on my Gardner house?
faqs.a: Gardner requires permits for many projects, including re-roofing, basement finishing, decks, fences, sheds and pools. If you cannot find the permit for earlier work, tell the buyer and ask the city's Building and Inspections office what records exist.

faqs.q: When are Johnson County property taxes due if I sell in the spring?
faqs.a: The first half or full payment is due December 20 and the second half May 10. At a spring closing, the title company usually shows whether the second half is paid and prorates what remains.
